BlaÅ¾ys / LRT The Prosecutor Generalâs Office has sent LRT a list of questions about the way its journalists conduct investigations by secretly recording actions or conversations, with some experts saying the move resembled signs of censorship. âI cannot understand such a request because it certainly does not comply with the principles of freedom of expression or, more broadly, those of the media in a democratic state,â said Toma BirmontienÄ, a professor at Mykolas Romeris University and a former Constitutional Court judge. In September, the Prosecutor Generalâs Office sent a detailed list of 15 questions to LRT, asking how covert recordings are regulated internally The office said it opened an investigation on its own initiative to protect the public interest. The decision followed an ongoing criminal investigation into a recording pen allegedly left by an LRT journalist at a social democrat meeting. âFrankly, I see this situation as censorship â an attempt to censor, an attempt to control, to find some other mechanism. The other mechanisms for exerting control have failed, so the impression is that this is the second act in a long-running play,â BirmontienÄ said in reference to the months-long protests over the independence of the public broadcaster. The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) on Wednesday also said it was worried about the investigation, saying it posed a risk to investigative journalism. âStrange curiosityâ Deimantas Jastramskis, a professor at Vilnius Universityâs Faculty of Communication and a member of the supervisory LRT Council, pointed out that the prosecution does not specify the context or purpose of its investigation in the letter. âIt seems even stranger when we consider the context in which LRT and the media have been operating for the past year or longer, and the fact that politicians have been directing all kinds of requests to LRT through various agencies. LRTâs Editorial Policy allows journalists to gather information covertly when there is evidence that the conduct they seek to document would demonstrate unlawful or dishonest actions by individuals, where there is a clear public interest in exposing them and informing the public. Journalists must also obtain prior approval from the editor responsible. âIf the letter were linked to a specific case or complaint, everything would be clear, and its purpose would be easier to understand,â Jastramskis told LRT.lt. The professor said the letter could be interpreted as an indirect reproach to journalists who seek to defend the public interest through their work. âI would describe this as a completely ill-considered move by the Prosecutor Generalâs Office,â he said. Journalists should not be afraid to make covert recordings when necessary, according to Jastramskis. âThe letter from the prosecution is relevant not only to LRT but to the entire media sector engaged in serious journalism. It suggests that journalists should have to justify themselves, explain their actions and answer even absurd questions simply because they are trying to serve the public interest,â he said. LRT | D. Umbrasas / LRT An abstract request DÅ¾ina DonauskaitÄ, head of the Lithuanian Centre for Journalism and an expert at Vilnius Universityâs Faculty of Communication, said the prosecutorâs request raised questions about why the inquiry was launched. âDid the prosecutor simply read LRTâs editorial policy guidelines and decide to check whether they were contrary to the public interest? Or is the Prosecutor Generalâs Office trying to find out how the media operate? âWhy is it trying to find out how the media work â out of curiosity or for other reasons? The prosecutionâs request is very vague, and it is unclear why it was made or in what context. It looks like pressure on the media,â DonauskaitÄ told LRT.lt. LRT has faced considerable pressure from various institutions in recent years, which raised further suspicions, she added. According to DonauskaitÄ, the letter amounts to interference in the organisationâs internal procedures and journalistic methods. âSince when has the prosecution been checking organisationsâ internal procedures?â she added. Common practice Freedom to conduct investigative journalism is particularly important, DonauskairtÄ said, adding that journalistsâ ability to do their work without it would be restricted. âThis is not in the interests of the prosecution itself or law enforcement agencies more broadly, because recent journalistic investigations, including those conducted with international partners, have shown that such investigations prompt law enforcement agencies to initiate numerous legal proceedings against institutions or organisations where corruption or violations of the public interest have occurred. âIf journalists cannot work freely, their investigations will fail to resonate with audiences. This is a way of preventing questions from being asked and obstructing journalistsâ work in an attempt to put pressure on them,â DonauskaitÄ said. Jastramskis, the Vilnius University professor, also said that journalists in all democratic countries use covert recordings in their investigations. âThis is necessary when the public interest requires a certain degree of intrusion into privacy,â Jastramskis said. The public interest Journalists have used covert recording in numerous investigations. For example, journalists from Info TV used the technique in an investigation into then MP KÄstutis PÅ«kas, who sexually harassed women applying to become parliamentary assistants. In considering the use of covert recording equipment to obtain some of the information, the Constitutional Court ruled that the Constitution guarantees and protects the public interest in being informed. It also stated that the public has more than sufficient grounds to want to know more about people involved in public or political life than about others. The General Prosecutor's Office | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT The Constitutional Court also noted that the media may inform the public about a public figure without their consent to the extent that the personâs personal characteristics, behaviour or other circumstances of their private life may have implications for public affairs, making the information published a matter of public interest. In its ruling, the Constitutional Court also referred to judgments by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which has found that unjustified restrictions would prevent the media from fulfilling their role as a âpublic watchdogâ. Professor Jastramskis also points out that various newsrooms have their own editorial standards, which they have clearly set out. He says the existing rules governing covert recording are sufficient. âYou can always regulate many things in greater detail, but more detailed regulation carries risks. If we regulate everything, we will become quite constrained. [...] We have the Lukashenko regime next door, where everything is certainly regulated.â âThe current rules stipulate that such activity must be approved by an editor. Would it make any difference if they additionally required everything to be sent by email or a form to be completed? What would that change in practice? Nothing,â Jastramskis said. Protecting public interest â prosecutors Last week, Elena MartinonienÄ, head of the Communications Division at the Prosecutor Generalâs Office, told LRT.lt that the investigation had been launched on a prosecutorâs initiative. The aim is to assess whether the provisions of LRTâs Editorial Policy allowing covert information gathering safeguard the constitutional right to respect for private life and comply with the relevant legislation governing the media and covert information gathering. MartinonienÄ said the prosecution disagreed that the investigation posed a threat to journalistsâ freedom. âIn the prosecutionâs view, journalistsâ freedom and the public interest are safeguarded precisely when the editorial rules governing journalistsâ work raise no doubts about their compliance with the Lithuanian Constitution and the law,â she said. âOnly after all the information necessary for the assessment has been received will a decision be made on whether there are grounds in this case to apply the measures provided for by law to protect the public interest,â MartinonienÄ added. https://www.dw.com/en/brutal-revolutiona.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OOrI A huge, highly revered golden statue of Genghis Khan is found in Mongolia's Chinggis Khaan National Museum, which opened in October 2022 Image: Chinggis Khaan National Museum Advertisement Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history. The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition " Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols ." The power of a disruptive individual The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project. "What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW. The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?" In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader. "If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says. Genghis Khan is revered in Mongolia as the founding father of the nation who united the warring steppe tribes. This statue is in the Parliament Building in the country's capital, Ulan Bator Image: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images The founder of the world's largest empire Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager. Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206. At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area. Nomadic culture, with yurt tents, traditional costumes and music instruments is celebrated here in Mongolia's 'Mongols Nomadic Winter Festival' Image: AFP Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000. Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy. A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system. Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency. A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion. Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer. The 'paiza' acted as the world's earliest form of passport, granting official travelers protection and safe passage across Eurasia Image: Uuganbaatar Otgonbaatar/Chinggis Khaan National Museum, Ulaanbaatar The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica." But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff. Shifting centers of power The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland. It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods. There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff. European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies. "When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched." The Mongols also used deception to confuse and trap their opponents Image: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin – Preußischer Kulturbesitz, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 71 S. 58 The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today. For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance. "In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula. Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes. But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today." The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.
